findings.rationale: The session token (a bearer credential) is persisted in sessionStorage, which is readable by any JavaScript running in the origin. An XSS or malicious third-party script can exfiltrate the token and hijack the session; HttpOnly/Secure cookies or in-memory storage would avoid this exposure.

recall() reads the credential back from user-controllable client storage. Any code (or an attacker who can write to sessionStorage) can supply or read this token, so it must never be treated as a trusted authentication/authorization assertion on the client.

A fragment of the session token is persisted in sessionStorage, which is readable by any JavaScript running in the origin (e.g. via XSS or a compromised third-party script). Since the comment states the backend resumes the session from this stored reference, the stored value is effectively a bearer credential living in browser storage; truncating it to 8 characters also drastically reduces its entropy, making it guessable/brute-forceable. Session credentials should be kept in HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies rather than web storage.
